state.misconception_label: Thinks alternate angles are always equal

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: Tom and Katie are arguing about alternate angles. Tom says angles \( p \) and \( q \) are alternate. Katie says angles \( p \) and \( q \) are equal. Who is correct? ![Shows two non parallel lines that are intersected by another line. Angles P and Q are both on the outside of the lines and on opposite sides of the transversal.](). I got Only
Katie because I assumed all the angles in the figure are equal.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you and a friend standing on opposite sides of a street, with a car passing by as the transversal. If you both point towards the car, are your arms at the same angle? Remember, alternate angles are not always equal, they are just congruent when lines are parallel.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh right, so if the street isn't straight, like if it's bent, then our arms wouldn't be at the same angle even though they're on opposite sides? So alternate angles are only equal when the two lines are actually parallel to each other?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: That's exactly right! Just like how your arms wouldn't be at the same angle if the street is bent, alternate angles are only equal when the lines are parallel. So in the case of Tom and Katie's argument, Katie is correct because the lines in the figure are not parallel. Keep up the great thinking!

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Wait, I'm a bit confused now - you said Katie is correct because the lines aren't parallel, but doesn't that mean the angles aren't equal? So shouldn't Tom be the one who's correct since he's just saying they're alternate angles, not that they're equal?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher effectively addresses the misconception that alternate angles are always equal, and the student shows clear progress in understanding, but the teacher makes a critical error in Turn 3 by incorrectly stating that Katie is correct when Tom should be correct (the angles are alternate but not equal since lines aren't parallel).
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses a concrete real-world analogy (people standing on opposite sides of a street pointing at a passing car) to explain the abstract concept of alternate angles and their relationship to parallel lines, which is a textbook example of the experiential strategy.
